title: Nakkai

paragraphs: He is mentioned in Jerusalem Talmud Maaser Sheni 2:2 as supplied [compare 5:2], as an attendant in Temple times, with the place wording ‘(in Migdol) Tzabbaya’; some say he was a scribe.
Hyman cites Samuel Krauss’s lexicon, page 366, for the description of Nakkai as a master of tradition in the time of the Tannaim.

notes.text: The connected wording שמש (במגדול) צבעא may designate service in Migdal Tzabbaya; it does not securely establish a profession as a dyer. The cited Maaser Sheni passage was not located in the bounded check. The lexicon author’s printed initials and surname remain unresolved.

The saved whole Venice MaaserSheni5:2 scalar names Nakkai as שמש במגדל וצבעייא and alternatively ספר. It supersedes the earlier2:2 nonmatch while supplied2:2 remains visible. The vav between Migdol and Tzabbaya leaves the place parsing open; no separate dyer profession is asserted. This is not proof of a printed chapter-letter change. SeferHaMilim, author הרר״ש קרוקס, page366 and the master-of-tradition claim remain Hyman’s unverified bibliographic report, without redundant guessed Rabbi initials or a silently identified Masorete.

The parallel is in Jerusalem Talmud Maaser Sheni 5:2. The Guggenheimer text gives Migdal Tzabbayah without a conjunction, while the Venice text has a conjunction. Both give an attendant and, in an alternate account, a scribe. The lexicon listed by Hyman as Sefer HaMilim by הרר״ש קרוקס is Samuel Krauss’s Greek and Latin Loanwords in the Talmud, Midrash and Targum (vol. II, 1899, p. 366). Krauss calls Nakkai a Masorete of the Tannaitic period and refers to Wilhelm Bacher for the description of him as the earliest link in the Masoretic chain.
